blocks.prompt: The Hedgehog With Five Thousand Spines
blocks.text: A hedgehog is not a porcupine, and it is not a rodent. It is a small night animal with about five thousand spines on its back. Each spine is hollow and stiff. It is made of keratin, the same stuff as your fingernails. A hedgehog cannot shoot its spines. Instead it has a ring of muscle around the edge of its back. When the hedgehog is frightened, that muscle pulls tight like the string on a purse. The hedgehog folds its head and legs inside, and it becomes a ball no fox wants to chew.

blocks.prompt: How the Hedgehog Got Its Name
blocks.text: A hedgehog spends the day asleep under a pile of leaves. At dusk it wakes, stretches, and goes hunting. It cannot see well, so it hunts with its nose and its ears. It pushes through grass, snuffling and grunting, listening for beetles, worms, and slugs. That grunting is where half its name comes from. It sounds like a tiny pig, and it forages along hedges, so people called it a hedgehog. A baby hedgehog is called a hoglet. Here is the clever part. A hoglet is born with its spines already grown, but they are hidden under a layer of puffy skin filled with fluid. That soft cover protects the mother while the babies are being born. Within a few hours the skin shrinks back and the first white spines push through. Over the next weeks, darker spines grow in around them. A grown hedgehog carries about five thousand spines. Each one lasts about a year, then falls out and a new one grows in its place.

blocks.prompt: The Strangest Thing a Hedgehog Does
blocks.text: Everyone knows the ball. Threaten a hedgehog and it tucks its head down, pulls its legs in, and draws a ring of muscle tight around the edge of its back until it is a spiny sphere with no soft part left showing. The muscle works like the drawstring on a bag. A fox can roll the ball around all night and get nothing for it. But the strangest thing a hedgehog does has no clear explanation at all. Give a hedgehog a new smell, a strong one, and it may begin to chew. It chews and chews until its mouth fills with froth. Then it twists its head around and paints that froth across its own spines with its tongue, reaching parts of its back you would think it could not reach. Scientists call this self-anointing. Nobody is certain why hedgehogs do it. Some think the foam makes them taste bad. Some think it hides their scent. Some think it is closer to a habit than a plan. Hedgehogs have another quiet advantage. Their muscles contain a protein that blocks some snake venom, so a hedgehog can take a bite from an adder that would kill an animal its size. It does not make them safe. It makes them harder to finish. In cold places, hedgehogs hibernate. A hibernating hedgehog lets its body go almost as cold as the air around it. Its heart slows from about one hundred and ninety beats a minute to around twenty. It looks dead. It is not. It is waiting for spring.

blocks.prompt: The Apple Myth and the Fence Problem
blocks.text: Pliny the Elder, writing in Rome almost two thousand years ago, reported that hedgehogs gathered fallen apples by rolling on them and carrying the fruit away stuck on their spines. It is a wonderful image. It is also wrong. Hedgehogs eat beetles, worms, caterpillars, and slugs, and an apple on the back would be no use to an animal that cannot reach it. Yet the story survived for centuries, copied from book to book, because nobody checked and everybody liked it. What hedgehogs actually do is less charming and more impressive. A European hedgehog may cover a mile or more in a single night, nose down, snuffling along hedges and ditches, hunting until dawn. Its eyes are poor. Its nose and ears do the work. When winter closes in, it builds a nest of leaves and shuts itself down: body temperature dropping to near the air temperature, heartbeat falling from roughly one hundred ninety beats a minute to twenty, breathing so shallow you would swear it had died. It wakes now and then, briefly, then sleeps again until spring. The trouble is that hedgehogs are built for a landscape that is disappearing. They need hedges, rough grass, leaf piles, and above all room to roam. Modern yards are tidy, and they are fenced. A solid fence with no gap at the bottom turns a garden into an island, and an island is no use to an animal that needs to walk a mile a night to eat. British hedgehog numbers have fallen sharply since the 1950s. In 2024 the European hedgehog was listed as Near Threatened on the international Red List. The fix, oddly, is small. People cut a gap the size of a fist in the base of the fence and call it a hedgehog highway. Dozens of connected gardens become one territory again. It is one of the few conservation problems in the world that an ordinary person can partly solve with a saw on a Saturday morning.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Order Eulipotyphla: closer to shrews and moles than to rodents
Convergent evolution with porcupines and echidnas
Each spine is a hollow keratin tube with internal braces
The orbicularis muscle closes the ball like a drawstring
Spines double as shock absorbers in a fall
Near Threatened as of 2024

blocks.prompt: Three Animals, One Answer
blocks.text: Look at a hedgehog, a porcupine, and an echidna side by side and you would swear they were cousins. All three are small, round, and covered in spines. None of them are closely related. The hedgehog is an insect eater, closer to shrews and moles than to anything else. The porcupine is a rodent, a relative of rats and beavers. The echidna is a monotreme, an egg-laying mammal whose nearest living relative is the platypus. The lines that led to them separated long before any of them existed, in some cases more than a hundred million years ago. Then, independently, each one arrived at the same answer: grow hairs, make them stiff, point them outward. Biologists call this convergent evolution. When a problem has one good solution, evolution keeps finding it, from different directions, with no coordination at all. The three did not build the same spine, though. A porcupine's quill is barbed at the tip and detaches on contact, which is why it ends up in a dog's face. A hedgehog's spine does neither. It stays attached, it carries no barbs, and it is closer to a piece of engineering than to a weapon. Each spine is a hollow tube of keratin, the same protein in your fingernails, braced on the inside by thin plates that keep it from crumpling. At its base is a narrow, flexible neck seated in a small ball of muscle. That neck lets the spine bend and spring back rather than snap, and it soaks up shock. This is why a hedgehog can fall from a height that would injure a similar animal and simply walk away. It lands on five thousand tiny shock absorbers. The rolling is the other half of the system. Around the rim of the hedgehog's spiny back runs a circular muscle, the orbicularis, working like the drawstring on a purse. When it contracts, the spiny skin is hauled down and inward over the head, the flanks, and the rump, and the soft face, belly, and legs disappear inside. What remains is a sphere with no handle and no seam. A fox can bat it, roll it, and mouth it, and unless it has extraordinary patience, the hedgehog does not much care. Here is the part worth arguing about. This animal, superbly defended against everything that hunts it, is in trouble anyway. British hedgehog numbers have collapsed since the 1950s, and in 2024 the European hedgehog was listed as Near Threatened. Nothing ate them. The landscape simply changed. Hedgerows were pulled out to make larger fields. Rough ground was mowed flat. Gardens were sealed with solid fence panels driven into the soil, and an animal that needs to walk a mile a night found itself closed inside a rectangle of lawn. Roads finished the job. The spines answer a fox. They have no answer for a fence. That is the uncomfortable lesson buried inside an animal we usually file under cute. An adaptation is only ever an answer to the world that shaped it, and we are changing the world far faster than the answers can be rewritten.
